body.stem: You have drafted three new subnets for an existing virtual network (IPv4 address space 10.30.0.0/16, East US 2, subscription Contoso-Prod) that today holds only a gateway subnet. You need Azure to accept every range as a valid, non-overlapping subnet range, and each subnet must be able to host the workload listed with room left for growth. Which change should you make to the draft before you submit it?

rows: SQL VM, cache VM, monitoring agent, backup agent

options.text: Set the data-tier address range to 10.30.9.64/28
Set the data-tier address range to 10.30.9.64/30
Set the data-tier address range to 10.30.9.128/29
Set the app-tier address range to 10.30.8.16/26

explanation.correct: A /29 range provides eight addresses, and Azure reserves the first and the last address for protocol conformance plus three more for Azure service use, leaving only three usable addresses. The data-tier subnet must host four workloads (SQL VM, cache VM, monitoring agent, backup agent) and still leave room for growth, so the drafted /29 is too small. Widening data-tier to 10.30.9.64/28 keeps the range inside the virtual network's 10.30.0.0/16 address space, stays clear of app-tier's 10.30.9.0/26 (which ends at 10.30.9.63), and raises usable capacity to eleven addresses, enough for the planned workloads plus growth.

perChoice.b: A /30 range is smaller than the smallest subnet range Azure accepts, which is /29, so this request is rejected outright before any capacity question arises.
perChoice.c: Relocating the subnet does not change its size: 10.30.9.128/29 is still eight addresses with five reserved by Azure, so only three usable addresses remain, which cannot hold the four planned workloads plus growth.
perChoice.d: A /26 at 10.30.8.16 spans 10.30.8.16 through 10.30.8.79, which falls inside the appgw range of 10.30.8.0/24 (10.30.8.0 through 10.30.8.255). Azure rejects subnet ranges that overlap inside the same virtual network, and this change also leaves data-tier at three usable addresses.

body.stem: You have a virtual network that contains a single subnet named `integration`, and that subnet holds two private endpoints (one for Azure Storage and one for Azure Key Vault). The security team wants the network security group and route table that already protect this subnet to also protect every private endpoint inside it, so that one set of rules covers the whole subnet. Which change should you make to the subnet?

options.text: Enable network policies for private endpoints on the subnet so that the subnet's network security group and route table apply to every private endpoint in it.
Enable the service endpoints for Azure Storage and Azure Key Vault services on the subnet so that every resource of those services can accept traffic from it.
Enable subnet delegation to Microsoft.Network/privateEndpoints so that the platform creates and manages the private endpoint network interfaces inside the delegated subnet.
Move the private endpoints into a separate subnet that has its own network security group and route table, leaving the current subnet and its controls unchanged.

explanation.correct: Turning on the subnet's setting for network policies on private endpoints makes the network security group and route table assigned to that subnet apply to every private endpoint deployed in it. Because the requirement is that the existing controls in the `integration` subnet cover the private endpoints that live there, enabling this setting at subnet scope is the change that satisfies it.

perChoice.b: Service endpoints solve a different problem: the Azure service keeps its public endpoint and Azure restricts access to that public endpoint to your VNet, and each resource of the service (for example each Storage account) must separately be permitted to accept traffic from the subnet. They do not extend the subnet's network security group or route table to private endpoints, so they do not deliver the single set of rules the security team asked for.
perChoice.c: Subnet delegation grants one service permission to create its own service-specific resources in the subnet during deployment; it is not a way of extending the subnet's network security group or route table to private endpoints. Delegation also cannot be added or removed while resources of the delegated service are already deployed in the subnet, so it is the wrong lever for this goal.
perChoice.d: Relocating the private endpoints to another subnet that carries different controls leaves the network security group and route table in the `integration` subnet unchanged, so the endpoints still would not be covered by the protections already in force for that subnet. Moving resources also adds work without meeting the stated requirement.

body.stem: You created the virtual network `app-vnet` through the portal last week and deployed two Linux virtual machines into its `app` subnet. The machines reach each other and resolve Azure service names, but every attempt to open a connection to an internet-hosted service fails, and the team does not want public IP addresses on the virtual machines. You need outbound internet connectivity for these virtual machines. Which change should you make?

options.text: Add a NAT gateway to the `app` subnet
Add a service endpoint for Azure Storage to the `app` subnet
Create a virtual network peering from `app-vnet` to the `shared-services` virtual network
Enable the private endpoints network policy setting on the `app` subnet

explanation.correct: Virtual networks created through the portal, and by API versions released after March 31, 2026, are created with `defaultOutboundAccess` set to `false`, so their subnets are private by default and the virtual machines get no implicit outbound public IP. The output shows exactly that state for `app-vnet`: `defaultOutboundAccess` is false and the network interface of `nic-app-01` has no public IP address, which is why the machines can reach each other but nothing on the internet. Virtual machines in such a subnet need an explicit outbound method — a NAT gateway associated with the subnet, a public IP on the network interface, or a public load balancer with outbound rules. Because the requirement rules out public IP addresses on the virtual machines, associating a NAT gateway with the `app` subnet is the change that restores outbound connectivity; the NAT gateway must be created in the same subscription and region as the virtual network.

perChoice.b: Service endpoints leave the service's own public endpoint in place and simply restrict it to your virtual network; enabling the Azure Storage endpoint only affects traffic that is destined for Azure Storage. It does not give the virtual machines a general path out to internet-hosted services and does not change the subnet's lack of an outbound method.
perChoice.c: Virtual network peering links two virtual networks so the resources on either side can communicate with each other, in the same or different regions and even across subscriptions. It is not an outbound connectivity method for the virtual machines in the `app` subnet, so it does not restore their access to the internet.
perChoice.d: The private endpoints network policy setting is what makes a subnet's network security group and route table apply to the private endpoints placed inside that subnet. The `app` subnet has no network security group, no route table and no private endpoints, and this setting has no effect on the outbound connectivity of ordinary virtual machines.

body.stem: You have a virtual network `data-vnet` with a subnet `svc-subnet` that holds two Linux virtual machines. An application on those machines reads from the storage account `contosodata`. The subnet has the Microsoft.Storage service endpoint turned on, but the machines time out whenever they reach the account. You need the machines in `svc-subnet` to reach `contosodata` again while keeping the account reachable only from that subnet. Which change should you make?

rows: Traffic from the virtual machines to `contosodata`

options.text: In the `contosodata` storage account, allow the `svc-subnet` subnet of the `data-vnet` virtual network.
In the `contosodata` storage account, change public network access to allow all networks instead of the subnet list.
In the `data-vnet` virtual network, remove the Microsoft.Storage service endpoint from `svc-subnet`.
In the `data-vnet` virtual network, attach a route table to `svc-subnet` and enable a default route to the internet.

explanation.correct: Turning on the service endpoint for Microsoft.Storage on `svc-subnet` only creates the VNet-scoped path to the storage service; each storage account that should accept traffic must separately permit the subnet. Because `contosodata` currently lists no allowed virtual networks, the change needed is to add `svc-subnet` (in `data-vnet`) to the allowed list on that storage account. The account keeps its public endpoint, but access is confined to the virtual network.

perChoice.b: Switching the account to allow all networks exposes `contosodata` to traffic from the public internet, which contradicts the requirement that only the subnet in `data-vnet` may reach it. The point of the service endpoint is to keep the service's public endpoint while limiting it to your virtual network.
perChoice.c: Removing the endpoint discards the VNet-scoped restriction and sends storage traffic out over the public path, so the account would no longer be locked to `svc-subnet`. It also does not make the subnet an accepted caller on the account itself.
perChoice.d: A route table only decides the next hop for traffic; it does not make the storage account accept connections from the subnet. The account-side permission for the subnet is what must change, and replacing the endpoint's path with a default route to the internet would also move storage traffic away from the VNet-scoped route.

body.stem: You have just replaced the DNS server list on the virtual network `corp-vnet` with the corporate resolvers `10.40.0.4` and `10.40.0.5`, because the Azure-provided DNS server can resolve names only inside the virtual network. The workloads sitting in that network are still answering from the old resolver, so the applications hosted there fail to find the on-premises services they depend on, such as `api.corp.contoso.com`. You need every workload in `corp-vnet` to use the new resolvers, and the network itself must not be rebuilt. Which action should you take?

exhibit.text:
Resource in corp-vnet                   | Resource type                  | Name resolution currently in use
---------------------------------------+--------------------------------+-------------------------------------------
corp-vnet (10.40.0.0/16, West Europe)   | Virtual network DNS server list | Changed today to 10.40.0.4 and 10.40.0.5
vm-app-01                               | Virtual machine (Linux)         | Azure-provided DNS server
vm-app-02                               | Virtual machine (Windows)       | Azure-provided DNS server
fw-app                                   | Azure Firewall                  | Azure-provided DNS server
agw-app                                  | Application Gateway             | Azure-provided DNS server

options.text: Restart the virtual machines, the Azure Firewall and the Application Gateway so they load the new DNS settings.
Recreate the virtual network with the new DNS settings and redeploy every workload into it.
Wait for the new DNS settings to propagate by themselves to the virtual machines, the Azure Firewall and the Application Gateway.
Remove the DNS server list from the virtual network so the virtual machines, the Azure Firewall and the Application Gateway fall back to the Azure-provided DNS server.

explanation.correct: Changing the DNS servers on a virtual network does not reconfigure the resources that are already running inside it. Virtual machines, Azure Firewalls and Application Gateways keep the DNS settings they had until they are restarted, so restarting each of the workloads listed in the exhibit is what makes them use the new resolvers 10.40.0.4 and 10.40.0.5. This satisfies the requirement without rebuilding the virtual network.

perChoice.b: Recreating the virtual network would throw away and rebuild every workload, which the requirement rules out. The new resolver list can be put into effect on the resources that are already running, so there is no need to redeploy anything.
perChoice.c: The DNS change is not pushed to running resources automatically. Virtual machines, Azure Firewalls and Application Gateways continue using their previous DNS settings until they are restarted, so waiting on propagation leaves the name-resolution failure in place.
perChoice.d: Removing the DNS server list returns the workloads to the Azure-provided DNS server, which resolves names only within the virtual network and is exactly the configuration that could not resolve the on-premises names. The goal is to use the two corporate resolvers, not to fall back to the default one.

body.stem: You have a subnet named `aks-subnet` inside the virtual network `hub-vnet`. The platform team wants to retire the AKS cluster that runs there and hand the subnet over to a service that requires its own delegation, but every attempt to change the subnet's delegation is rejected and the subnet stays tied to the current service. You need the delegation removed so the subnet can be reused, without changing any address space. Which sequence of actions should you take?

exhibit.text:
Virtual network : hub-vnet   (10.70.0.0/16, East US 2)
Subnet          : aks-subnet   (10.70.10.0/24)
Delegation      : Microsoft.ContainerService/managedClusters
In aks-subnet   : AKS cluster hub-aks (control plane, node pool np-01 with 3 nodes)
build-subnet    : 10.70.20.0/24 - 1 build agent virtual machine, no delegation

options.text: Delete the AKS cluster and its resources from `aks-subnet`, and then remove the delegation from the subnet.
Remove the delegation from `aks-subnet`, and then delete the AKS cluster and its resources.
Create a second subnet with the same address range and the same delegation, then delete the original subnet and its resources.
Delete only the worker node pool of the AKS cluster, and then remove the delegation from `aks-subnet`.

explanation.correct: Azure refuses to add or remove a delegation on a subnet that still holds resources of the delegated service. The exhibit shows that `aks-subnet` is delegated to Microsoft.ContainerService/managedClusters and still hosts the AKS cluster `hub-aks` (control plane and node pool np-01). Removing that cluster and its resources from the subnet clears the condition, after which the delegation can be removed and the subnet handed over to the new service, which satisfies the goal of retiring the cluster and reusing the subnet without touching any address space.

perChoice.b: This reverses the required order. While the AKS cluster and its node resources are still deployed in `aks-subnet`, the platform rejects removal of the delegation, so the deletion of the cluster would never be reached in a working sequence.
perChoice.c: Two subnets inside one virtual network cannot hold overlapping address ranges, so a second subnet cannot be created with 10.70.10.0/24, and the original subnet cannot be deleted while it still holds resources. The approach also leaves the delegation in place on the replacement subnet, which is the opposite of the stated goal.
perChoice.d: Deleting the worker node pool still leaves the AKS cluster itself deployed in `aks-subnet`, so the removal of the delegation continues to be rejected. Every resource of the delegated service must be cleared out of the subnet first.

body.stem: You have the virtual network `hub-vnet` in subscription Contoso-Prod, whose IPv4 address space is currently 10.50.0.0/16 and which holds two subnets. The IPAM team wants a second IPv4 address range added to this network so that a new `partner` subnet can later host roughly 40 virtual machines with room for growth, but the range they submitted, 169.254.0.0/24, is refused by Azure. You need to hand the IPAM team a replacement range that Azure will accept and that stays clear of the address space already in use. Which range should you request?

explanation.correct: 172.20.0.0/20 is a private RFC 1918 range that Azure accepts, and it does not clash with the space the network already uses: the network's existing range is 10.50.0.0/16 and both current subnets sit inside that range, so a range drawn from 172.20.0.0/16 can be added as a second address space while the existing range and subnets remain untouched. At /20 it also provides far more addresses than the roughly 40 virtual machines the planned `partner` subnet needs, leaving room for growth, whereas the submitted 169.254.0.0/24 falls in the link-local space that Azure never allows in a virtual network's address space.

perChoice.a: 10.50.128.0/24 sits inside 10.50.0.0/16, the range this virtual network already uses, so adding it would put two overlapping ranges in the same address space. A virtual network's IPv4 address space is one or more non-overlapping CIDR ranges, and any new range must also stay clear of space used by peered networks or on-premises networks.
perChoice.b: 224.0.0.0/4 is the multicast range, one of the ranges Azure never lets you add to a virtual network, so the request would be turned down no matter how the partner subnet is sized.
perChoice.d: 168.63.129.16/32 is the single address Azure keeps for its own internal DNS, DHCP and Load Balancer health probes, so it cannot become part of a virtual network's address space; on top of that, a single address leaves no room at all for the planned subnet.

body.stem: You have a Linux virtual machine `web-01` that runs in the `app` subnet of the virtual network `prod-vnet`. A redesign calls for the machine to run in the `app` subnet of `hub-vnet` instead, and the data on its OS disk has to survive the change. Which action should you take?

rows: an interface in the app subnet of hub-vnet
keep the data on the existing disk

options.text: Delete the virtual machine web-01 and create a replacement in the hub-vnet app subnet, reusing the existing managed OS disk and a new network interface in that subnet.
Move the existing network interface web-01-nic from the prod-vnet app subnet to the hub-vnet app subnet and attach it to the virtual machine web-01 so that it can reach the new hub services.
Move the existing virtual machine web-01 and its network interface into the hub-vnet app subnet, keeping the current OS disk and its data.
Create a new virtual machine in the hub-vnet app subnet with a new managed OS disk and a new network interface in that subnet.

explanation.correct: Azure has no in-place relocation for a virtual machine that must run in a different virtual network: the supported path is to remove the machine and build it again in the destination network, and the machine's disks can be carried over to the new machine. Because both virtual networks are in the same subscription and region, the managed disk `web-01-osdisk` can be reused. Deleting web-01 and creating a replacement in the hub-vnet `app` subnet, reattaching that existing managed OS disk and letting a new network interface be created in that subnet, keeps the data intact and puts the machine in the required subnet.

perChoice.b: An existing network interface cannot be transferred into another virtual network or subnet; it belongs to the network and subnet in which it was created. Relocating the workload into hub-vnet therefore requires the machine itself to be removed and rebuilt there, so shifting only the interface does not accomplish the move.
perChoice.c: Azure does not move a virtual machine into another virtual network. Peering or other connectivity between prod-vnet and hub-vnet would let the machine in prod-vnet reach hub-vnet, but the machine would still run in the prod-vnet `app` subnet, so the required placement is not met.
perChoice.d: Building the replacement machine with a brand-new managed OS disk starts from an empty disk, so the data on web-01-osdisk would be left behind rather than preserved. Keeping the data requires reusing the existing managed OS disk in the recreated machine.

body.stem: You administer the five subnets of the virtual network `corp-vnet` in East US 2 (subscription Contoso-Prod). The exhibit shows what each subnet holds today, and one request has been raised per subnet. For every request, drag the Azure setting or feature that delivers it into the matching slot.

rows: Two machines that terminate inbound traffic coming from the internet
Empty; reserved for a workload family that has not been deployed yet
Machines that today receive no default path to the internet
Perimeter workloads that partners connect to

slots.label: edge-snet — traffic leaving this subnet must be handed to a virtual appliance that inspects and forwards it instead of taking the most direct path to its destination.
web-snet — traffic flowing between the subnets that hold the three application tiers must be allowed or blocked by source IP, destination IP, port, and protocol.
int-snet — one Azure product must be able to place the objects it needs inside this subnet and have Azure manage them on that product's behalf.
ops-snet — machines created in this subnet must not come up with any default path to the internet; the team wants that absence to be a property of the subnet itself rather than left to chance.
dmz-snet — the perimeter tier has to hold resources that speak both IP versions; the extra version must be enabled once for the whole subnet instead of per resource.

explanation.correct: Each request is met by a different subnet-level control. The edge subnet needs explicit next hops so that outbound packets are handed to an appliance, which is what a route table provides. The application subnet needs rule-based allow/deny by source and destination IP, port, and protocol, which is the job of a network security group. The integration subnet must be handed to one product that then creates and owns its own resources there, which is subnet delegation. The operations subnet must be created so that new machines get no default path out, which is the private subnet option. The perimeter subnet must carry both IP versions for the whole subnet at once, which is adding an IPv6 address space. The remaining two candidates solve problems no request raises here.

perChoice.a: This belongs in the edge-snet slot: a route table overrides the default next hop for traffic leaving a subnet, so packets can be handed to a virtual appliance that inspects and forwards them.
perChoice.b: This belongs in the web-snet slot: a network security group is the rule-based allow/deny control that filters traffic inside the virtual network by source and destination IP, port, and protocol.
perChoice.c: This belongs in the int-snet slot: subnet delegation gives one product permission to create and own its own resources in the subnet during deployment, which is what the integration team asked for.
perChoice.d: This belongs in the ops-snet slot: the private subnet option blocks default outbound access for new virtual machines, so machines created in the subnet come up with no default path to the internet.
perChoice.e: This belongs in the dmz-snet slot: adding an IPv6 address space to the subnet enables the second IP version for the whole subnet, which is what the perimeter tier needs; keep in mind that not every product supports IPv6 yet.
perChoice.f: This fits none of the requests: it extends the rule set and next-hop rules already attached to a subnet to privately addressed resources placed in it, and no request in this exercise concerns those resources.
perChoice.g: This fits none of the requests: it supplies an explicit outbound path for machines in a subnet that has none, whereas the ops-snet request asks for the opposite — that new machines receive no default path out.

body.stem: You administer hub-vnet in East US 2 (subscription Contoso-Prod), where the reporting application runs, and the exhibit lists the environments and targets that have to connect to it. You need each of the six requests to be satisfied by exactly one of the options listed. Drag each option into the slot that states the request it satisfies.

exhibit.text:
Environment or target          | Current state
------------------------------|----------------------------------------------------------------
Developer laptops              | 8 staff working from home and on the road, without corporate hardware
Contoso head-office LAN        | 180 devices; the edge appliance on the perimeter supports IPsec tunnels
Contoso datacenter network     | A private circuit is contracted with a service provider
partner-vnet in another region | Hosts the partner's application
SQL database contosodl         | Queried by the reporting application that runs in hub-vnet
Storage account contosodata    | Reachable today over its public address from any network

slots.label: Give one developer laptop encrypted access into the virtual network, with no change needed at the office
Connect the whole on-premises office network with the cloud through an encrypted tunnel that starts at the edge appliance
Extend the on-premises datacenter network into the cloud over a partner circuit that never carries traffic across the internet
Let resources in partner-vnet and hub-vnet exchange traffic directly over the Azure backbone, even though the two sit in different regions
Reach a single instance of the reporting database over an internal address that is never exposed to the internet
Keep the storage account on its public address while accepting traffic only from inside the virtual network

explanation.correct: The developer laptop request is met by a point-to-site VPN, the whole head-office LAN request by a site-to-site VPN, the datacenter request by Azure ExpressRoute (a private partner circuit that never uses the internet), the partner environment request by virtual network peering across regions, the reporting database request by Azure Private Link on a fully private address, and the storage account request by service endpoints, which keep the account on its public address while restricting it to the virtual network.

perChoice.a: This belongs with the developer-laptop request: a point-to-site VPN gives a single computer encrypted access to the virtual network with few or no changes to the local network, which is exactly what travelling staff without corporate hardware need.
perChoice.b: This belongs with the head-office request: a site-to-site VPN connects the whole on-premises network, through the on-premises VPN device, to an Azure VPN gateway in the virtual network, so all 180 office devices reach Azure over one encrypted tunnel.
perChoice.c: This belongs with the datacenter request: ExpressRoute is a private circuit provided by a partner that never carries the traffic over the internet, which is what the contracted private circuit provides.
perChoice.d: This belongs with the partner request: peering links two virtual networks in the same or different regions so resources on either side can communicate directly, without any on-premises VPN involved.
perChoice.e: This belongs with the reporting database request: Private Link exposes a single instance of a service on a fully private IP, so the database is reached on an address that is never exposed to the internet.
perChoice.f: This belongs with the storage account request: service endpoints keep the service on its public endpoint and restrict it to the virtual network, after which subnet access is additionally enabled on the storage account itself.

body.stem: You have the draft address plan for a new virtual network, `pay-vnet`, that the Contoso platform team will build in West Europe (subscription Contoso-Prod). The IPAM team has allocated the IPv4 address space `10.60.0.0/16` for it, and each of the four application tiers will run in its own subnet. The exhibit lists how many virtual machines every tier runs today and how many it has to support at its peak. You need one address range per subnet so that Azure accepts every range in the plan, no two subnets overlap, and each tier still has room to grow. Which address range should you assign to each subnet? Drag the range into the matching slot.

exhibit.text:
Draft subnet plan for pay-vnet (allocated address space 10.60.0.0/16)

Tier          Subnet name         Machines today   Machines at peak
------------  ------------------  ---------------  ----------------
Web           web-snet           50               90
Application   app-snet           15               45
Data          data-snet           6               10
Integration   integration-snet    8               12

slots.label: Web tier subnet
Application tier subnet
Data tier subnet
Integration tier subnet

explanation.correct: Each subnet range must sit inside the allocated space 10.60.0.0/16, must not overlap any other subnet range, and must hold the tier's peak number of virtual machines with room to grow. Azure reserves five addresses in every subnet (the first and the last plus three for Azure services), so a /24 leaves 251 usable addresses, a /26 leaves 59, a /27 leaves 27 and a /28 leaves 11. That fixes the placement uniquely: the web tier (90 machines at peak) can only take the /24, the application tier (45 at peak) the /26, the data tier (10 at peak) the /28 and the integration tier (12 at peak) the /27, and none of those ranges overlap each other.

perChoice.i1: Correct for the Web tier subnet: the range lies inside 10.60.0.0/16, does not overlap the other three subnet ranges, and after the five addresses Azure reserves it still offers 251 usable addresses, comfortably covering the 90 virtual machines the tier must run at peak.
perChoice.i2: Correct for the Application tier subnet: the range is inside the allocated space and does not overlap the other subnets, and its 59 usable addresses cover the 45 machines the tier needs at peak while leaving growth headroom.
perChoice.i3: Correct for the Data tier subnet: the range sits inside the allocated space and leaves 11 usable addresses once Azure's five reserved addresses are taken out, which covers the 10 machines the tier must run at peak.
perChoice.i4: Correct for the Integration tier subnet: the range is inside the allocated space, does not overlap the other subnet ranges, and its 27 usable addresses cover the 12 machines needed at peak.
perChoice.i5: This range lies in 10.70.0.0/16, outside the space the IPAM team allocated for this network, so it cannot be used for any of the four subnets even though its size would otherwise fit the web tier.
perChoice.i6: This falls inside 169.254.0.0/16, the link-local range, which Azure never allows in a virtual network's address space, so it fits none of the subnets.
perChoice.i7: A /29 is the smallest range Azure accepts, and only three of its eight addresses remain usable after Azure's five reserved addresses, which is far too few for any of the four tiers.
perChoice.i8: 224.0.0.0/4 is the multicast range, which can never be added to a virtual network's address space, so it fits no subnet in this plan.

body.stem: You administer the virtual network `contoso-vnet` (West Europe, subscription Contoso-Prod). The IPAM team has raised four requests about the IPv4 address space of that network; the exhibit shows what the network holds today. Drag the operation that satisfies each request into the matching slot.

rows: 10.80.1.0/24, part of the 10.80.0.0/16 range, 6 virtual machines running
10.80.2.0/24, part of the 10.80.0.0/16 range, 3 virtual machines running
10.80.3.0/24, part of the 10.80.0.0/16 range, 1 VPN gateway
10.81.0.0/24, part of the 10.81.0.0/24 range, no virtual machines left

items.text: Widen the range to cover a larger block of addresses
Shrink the range only while it still covers every subnet range inside it
Delete every subnet in the range first, then remove the range
Create a separate virtual network and connect the two with peering
Move the subnets into a different virtual network and delete this one

slots.label: Reserve a range belonging to the staging environment, clear of the space that other networks already use
Make much more room within the main range, keeping the subnets exactly where they sit today
Reclaim the unused part of the main range; the running workloads must stay exactly where they are
Take the pilot range out of service now that the pilot workload is decommissioned

explanation.correct: All four requests are edits to the IPv4 address space of contoso-vnet itself. The staging environment needs a new range added to that address space, and a new range cannot overlap the ranges already defined in the network, the peered network (10.90.0.0/16) or the on-premises network (10.100.0.0/16). More room in the main range means extending that range, for example changing a /16 to a /8, which leaves every subnet where it is. Reclaiming unused space in the main range means decreasing it, and that is permitted only while the smaller range still includes the ranges of the subnets inside it, so the running workloads keep their addresses. Taking the pilot range out of service means removing it, and a range that still holds a subnet cannot be removed, so the subnet and any resources in it are deleted first.

perChoice.a: Fits the staging request: a new range is added to the address space of contoso-vnet, and it must not overlap the ranges already defined in that network, the peered network or the on-premises network, otherwise those networks can no longer be connected.
perChoice.b: Fits the request for more room: extending the main range, for example from /16 to /8, enlarges it without moving any subnet or workload. Decreasing the range would do the opposite of what is asked.
perChoice.c: Fits the request to reclaim unused space: the main range can be decreased only as long as the smaller range still includes the ranges of every subnet inside it, which is exactly what keeps the running workloads on the same addresses.
perChoice.d: Fits the request to retire the pilot range: a range that still holds a subnet cannot be removed, so the subnets and the resources in them are deleted first and only then is the range removed.
perChoice.e: Fits no slot: a second virtual network joined by peering gives the staging environment a separate address space, but these requests are changes to the address space of contoso-vnet, which is not being replaced here.
perChoice.f: Fits no slot: moving the subnets into a different virtual network relocates the workloads rather than editing the address space of contoso-vnet, and the requests keep the workloads on their current subnets.

body.stem: You have the virtual network `corp-vnet` in East US 2 (subscription Contoso-Prod), whose IPv4 address space is 10.10.0.0/16 and which is peered with `partner-vnet` (10.90.0.0/16). The exhibit lists five change requests raised against that network and its subnets, and Azure refused every one of them. You need to tell the requester what caused each refusal so the request can be corrected. Drag the cause of each refusal into the matching slot.

rows: Add a subnet named `data` with the range 10.30.0.0/24 to `corp-vnet`.
Change the name of the subnet `app` to `application-tier`.
The portal offers no editable field for the name, and the command returns an error.
Remove the `Microsoft.Web/serverFarms` delegation from the subnet `web`.
The delegation stays in place; the App Service plan `web-plan` is still deployed in that subnet.
Change the range of the subnet `db` from 10.10.3.0/24 to 10.10.3.0/22.
The update is refused; two virtual machines are running in that subnet.
The deletion is refused even though the subnet holds no resources; the network is still peered with another virtual network and a gateway connection remains active.

items.text: The range does not sit inside the address space that the virtual network covers.
The value fixed at creation time cannot be altered afterwards.
Resources of the service the subnet was delegated to are still deployed in it.
The subnet must be empty before its own address space can be altered.
Gateway connections, gateways, IP addresses, virtual network peerings, or an App Service Environment can block subnet operations.

slots.label: Attempt 1 — add the `data` subnet
Attempt 2 — rename the `app` subnet
Attempt 3 — free the `web` subnet for another service
Attempt 4 — widen the `db` subnet
Attempt 5 — remove the `legacy` subnet

explanation.correct: Each keyed placement pairs what the requester saw with the constraint that explains it. The new subnet range 10.30.0.0/24 falls outside corp-vnet's 10.10.0.0/16 space, and a subnet range must lie inside the address space of its virtual network (and must not overlap other ranges, which rules out the peer). A virtual network name and a subnet name are fixed when the resource is created and cannot be changed afterwards, so the `app` subnet cannot be renamed. A subnet delegation cannot be added or removed while resources of the delegated service are still deployed in the subnet, so `web-plan` has to be deleted before the `Microsoft.Web/serverFarms` delegation can be dropped. A subnet's address range can only be changed while the subnet is empty, and two virtual machines sit in `db`. Finally, adding, changing, or deleting a subnet can be blocked by gateway connections, gateways, IP addresses, virtual network peerings, and an App Service Environment, which is what stops the `legacy` deletion.

perChoice.i1: Belongs in Attempt 1: a subnet address range must lie inside the address space of its virtual network, and 10.30.0.0/24 is outside corp-vnet's 10.10.0.0/16 and does not overlap the peer either.
perChoice.i2: Belongs in Attempt 2: the virtual network name and the subnet name are chosen at creation and are immutable afterwards, so the `app` subnet cannot be renamed and must be replaced if a new name is required.
perChoice.i3: Belongs in Attempt 3: a delegation cannot be added or removed while resources of the delegated service are deployed in the subnet, so the App Service plan `web-plan` must be removed before the delegation can be dropped.
perChoice.i4: Belongs in Attempt 4: a subnet's address range can only be changed while the subnet holds no resources, so the two virtual machines in `db` must be moved or deleted first.
perChoice.i5: Belongs in Attempt 5: subnet creation, modification, and deletion can fail because of gateway connections, gateways, IP addresses, virtual network peerings, or an App Service Environment, and corp-vnet still has a peering and an active gateway connection even though `legacy` itself is empty.

body.stem: You are reworking name resolution for Contoso's virtual networks and the workloads that run in them. The exhibit lists the objects involved and the resolvers configured on them today. Drag the DNS configuration or the behaviour that satisfies each request into the matching slot.

rows: Virtual machine in the app subnet of app-vnet

items.text: The DNS settings on the network interface, which take precedence over those of the virtual network
The first server in the list that can be reached answers the query and the remaining servers are skipped
A removal that applies only to the list of one virtual network, leaving the other lists untouched
The DNS settings of the virtual network, which take precedence over those on the network interface
The servers in the list are used in a rotating pattern so the load is spread across them

slots.label: The names of resources that run inside `app-vnet` must resolve with no setup, and the team does not want to stand up any name-resolution infrastructure of its own.
Names of resources that run in `hub-vnet` must be resolvable from `corp-vnet`.
The virtual machine `web-01` must reach the corporate resolver 10.40.0.53 even though `app-vnet` keeps the built-in ones.
The two resolvers configured on `hub-vnet` must be consulted in the sequence they were entered, never in a changing order.
The resolver 10.40.0.4 must stop being used by `finance-vnet`, while `corp-vnet` and everything else that depends on it must keep working through it.

explanation.correct: The Azure-provided resolver handles names for resources connected to a single virtual network and needs no infrastructure of your own, so it fits app-vnet, which only has to resolve its own names (i1). The Azure-provided resolver cannot look up names in another virtual network, so corp-vnet must use custom DNS pointing at the corporate resolvers 10.40.0.4 and 10.40.0.5 to reach names in hub-vnet (i2). A network interface can carry its own DNS settings, and those override the ones set on the virtual network, so web-01 must carry 10.40.0.53 itself while app-vnet stays on the built-in ones (i3). Custom DNS servers are consulted in the order they appear in the list, not round-robin, so on hub-vnet the first reachable server answers and the others are skipped (i4). Deleting a resolver from one virtual network's list only removes it there; it stays registered with Azure for the other virtual networks that use it, so removing 10.40.0.4 from finance-vnet leaves corp-vnet working (i5).

perChoice.i1: Correct for app-vnet. The Azure-provided service registers resource names and private IP addresses automatically and resolves names between resources connected to the same virtual network, with no servers of your own to run, which is exactly what the request asks for.
perChoice.i2: Correct for corp-vnet. The built-in resolver cannot resolve names across virtual networks, so the corporate resolvers 10.40.0.4 and 10.40.0.5 have to be configured as custom DNS on the network for names in hub-vnet to resolve.
perChoice.i3: Correct for web-01. When a network interface has its own DNS server settings they take precedence over the settings configured on the virtual network, so the interface can use 10.40.0.53 while app-vnet keeps the built-in ones.
perChoice.i4: Correct for hub-vnet. Servers configured as custom DNS are used in the order they were entered; they do not work as a rotating set, so the first reachable server in the list handles the query and the remaining servers are not tried.
perChoice.i5: Correct for finance-vnet. Removing an address from the server list of a virtual network removes it only from that network's list; it stays registered with Azure for the other virtual networks that use it, so corp-vnet keeps resolving through 10.40.0.4.
perChoice.i6: This reverses the actual behaviour: the settings held on a network interface override those of the virtual network, not the other way round, so it satisfies none of the requests.
perChoice.i7: Servers listed as custom DNS are not used in a rotating pattern; they are consulted in the order they were entered, so this satisfies none of the requests.

body.stem: You administer the virtual network `hub-vnet` in the Contoso-Prod subscription in East US 2. Today the network carries a single IPv4 range and holds two running subnets, and the Contoso partner team plans to peer `partner-vnet` into it next quarter, so `hub-vnet` has to carry a second range that will not clash with the space the partner network occupies. IPAM has offered two candidate ranges for that second range, and the change must leave the range already in place along with both subnets. Which Azure CLI command should you run?
body.statement: The command that carries out this change is {{cmd}}.

options.text: az network vnet update --resource-group Contoso-Prod --name hub-vnet --address-prefixes 10.20.0.0/16 10.21.0.0/16
az network vnet update --resource-group Contoso-Prod --name hub-vnet --address-prefixes 10.20.0.0/16 10.30.0.0/16
az network vnet update --resource-group Contoso-Prod --name hub-vnet --address-prefixes 10.21.0.0/16
az network vnet create --resource-group Contoso-Prod --name hub-vnet --address-prefixes 10.20.0.0/16 10.21.0.0/16

explanation.correct: The `--address-prefixes` argument of `az network vnet update` overrides the address space of the network instead of appending to it, so the range already configured, `10.20.0.0/16`, must be listed again next to the new one. Of the two candidates, only `10.21.0.0/16` is free of a clash, because `10.30.0.0/16` is the address space that `partner-vnet` occupies and networks with overlapping ranges can never be connected by peering. Because `hub-vnet` already exists, the change is made with `az network vnet update` rather than with a creation command, and listing both ranges keeps the two running subnets inside the network's address space.

perChoice.cmd:b: This keeps the range already configured but adds `10.30.0.0/16`, which is exactly the address space of `partner-vnet`. Overlapping address spaces stop the two networks from ever being connected by peering or VPN, so the planned peering could not be created afterwards.
perChoice.cmd:c: Only the new range is listed, and because `--address-prefixes` overrides the previous ranges instead of adding to them, `10.20.0.0/16` would disappear from the network. The two subnets at `10.20.1.0/24` and `10.20.2.0/24` would then sit outside the network's address space.
perChoice.cmd:d: `az network vnet create` is for building a network that does not exist yet, and a virtual network name has to be unique within its resource group, so this command conflicts with the `hub-vnet` that is already there instead of changing its address space.

body.stem: You have been asked to design the network for the Contoso order platform in West Europe. The service has to keep running when a single availability zone is lost, and the plan pins each application tier to a different availability zone, as the exhibit shows. The platform team wants to avoid duplicating address space and connection relationships across the region, and every tier has to run in the availability zone given to it. Which approach should you take?

options.text: Create a single virtual network in West Europe with one subnet per tier and place each tier's virtual machines in the availability zone listed for that tier
Create one virtual network per availability zone in West Europe and add a subnet for every tier inside each of them
Create three virtual networks in West Europe, one for each tier, and add the availability zone to the address range of each
Create a single virtual network in West Europe with one subnet per tier and add an availability zone to the address range of each subnet

explanation.correct: A virtual network and all of its subnets span every availability zone in the region, so a single virtual network in West Europe can hold the three tiers in separate subnets while each tier's virtual machines are pinned to zone 1, 2 or 3. Nothing extra has to be created or configured per zone: the zone is simply chosen for each virtual machine when it is deployed, and the address ranges stay plain CIDR blocks inside the network's address space.

perChoice.slot1:b: Building one network per availability zone duplicates the address plan and the connections for the same three tiers, which is exactly what the team wants to avoid. It is also unnecessary, because a virtual network and its subnets already cover every zone in the region, so the tiers can share one network and still run in different zones.
perChoice.slot1:c: Zones cannot be attached to an address range; subnet address ranges are CIDR blocks that must sit inside the virtual network's address space, and the zone of a virtual machine is chosen at deployment time rather than inherited from the network. Splitting the tiers into three separate networks also multiplies the address space and the routing and peering work without any zonal benefit.
perChoice.slot1:d: Adding an availability zone to the address range of a subnet is not a supported setting, so this change would be rejected by Azure. The single network with one subnet per tier is already the correct design, and the zone each workload runs in comes from the virtual machine's own configuration, not from the subnet's range.

body.stem: You administer the virtual network `contoso-vnet` in East US 2 (subscription Contoso-Prod), and the exhibit shows how the network looks today. The platform team is trying to place an Azure Application Gateway in the subnet that already exists, but every attempt is refused with an error that points at the subnet itself rather than at any gateway setting. The three virtual machines that run in that subnet must keep working, the address space of the virtual network must stay exactly as it is, and the gateway has to end up serving traffic inside `contoso-vnet`. Which action should you take?

rows: Resource the team wants to add

body.statement: The action that puts the Azure Application Gateway inside `contoso-vnet` while the three virtual machines keep running and the address space stays as it is, is: {{slot1}}

options.text: Create a second subnet whose name starts with a letter and place the gateway in it
Rename the existing subnet so that its name starts with a letter and place the gateway in it
Create a second subnet whose name starts with a digit and place the gateway in it
Change the address range of the existing subnet and place the gateway in it

explanation.correct: The refusal comes from the subnet's name: Azure Application Gateway can only be deployed into a subnet whose name begins with a letter, and `10-appgw` begins with a digit. A subnet name cannot be changed after the subnet is created, and the address range of a subnet can only be edited while the subnet holds no resources, so with three virtual machines deployed in it neither renaming nor resizing that subnet is an option. The workable move is to add another subnet inside `contoso-vnet` whose name starts with a letter, give it a range taken from the existing 10.70.0.0/16 space (for example 10.70.2.0/24), and put the Application Gateway there, leaving `10-appgw` and its workloads untouched.

perChoice.slot1:b: Renaming is not possible: a subnet name is fixed at creation and cannot be changed afterwards, so `10-appgw` can never take a letter-first name.
perChoice.slot1:c: A name that begins with a digit reproduces exactly the condition Azure rejects, so the same refusal comes back.
perChoice.slot1:d: The address range of a subnet can only be changed while no resources are deployed in it; with three virtual machines running there the edit is refused, and a different range would not remove the naming problem in any case.

body.stem: You administer the virtual network `retail-vnet` and its `app` subnet in the East US 2 region of the Contoso-Prod subscription. Colleagues have already built the network security group, the route table and the NAT gateway that the `app` subnet is meant to use, as the exhibit shows, but Azure refuses every attempt to associate them with that subnet. You need the three objects associated with the `app` subnet, keeping the rules and the routes the team wrote and leaving the address space of the virtual network unchanged. Which action should you take?

exhibit.text:
Object                    Name          Subscription   Region
Virtual network           retail-vnet   Contoso-Prod   East US 2
Subnet in retail-vnet     app           Contoso-Prod   East US 2
Network security group    nsg-app       Contoso-Dev    West Europe
Route table               rt-app        Contoso-Dev    West Europe
NAT gateway               nat-app       Contoso-Prod   West Europe

body.statement: To make all three associations succeed, {{slot1}}.

options.text: create the three objects again in the Contoso-Prod subscription in the East US 2 region and associate those copies with the `app` subnet
create the three objects again in the Contoso-Prod subscription but in the West Europe region and associate those copies with the `app` subnet
create the three objects again in the Contoso-Dev subscription in the East US 2 region and associate those copies with the `app` subnet
ask Azure to copy the three objects into the Contoso-Prod subscription and the East US 2 region and associate the copies with the `app` subnet

explanation.correct: A network security group, a route table and a NAT gateway can only be associated with a subnet when the object already exists in the same subscription and the same location (region) as the virtual network it belongs to. `retail-vnet` sits in Contoso-Prod in East US 2, and each of the three objects is in the wrong place: `nsg-app` and `rt-app` are in another subscription, and `nat-app` is in another region. None of these objects can be moved across subscriptions or regions, so the team has to build replacements in the Contoso-Prod subscription in East US 2 and attach those, which keeps the subnet's address space and the rules and routes the team wrote.

perChoice.slot1:b: The subscription is right but the region is not: an object must also share the virtual network's location, so replacements built in West Europe are refused for a subnet of a virtual network in East US 2.
perChoice.slot1:c: The region is right but the subscription is not: the object must live in the same subscription as the virtual network, so a copy created in Contoso-Dev cannot be associated with a subnet of a virtual network owned by Contoso-Prod.
perChoice.slot1:d: Azure does not replicate a network security group, route table or NAT gateway into another subscription or region on request; each object has to be created in the subscription and region of the virtual network.

body.stem: You administer the virtual network `hub-vnet` in the Contoso-Prod subscription, and it holds the `app`, `data` and `integration` subnets. A junior engineer has to be able to create, change and remove the subnets of `hub-vnet`, to move virtual machines into and out of those subnets, and to switch on a service endpoint for one of them, but that same account must not be able to remove `hub-vnet` itself or to manage its peerings. Which access arrangement should you apply to the engineer's account?
body.statement: The access arrangement that satisfies every one of these requirements is {{slot0}}.

options.text: A custom role scoped to the virtual network that allows read, write, delete, join and joinViaServiceEndpoint on its subnets
Network Contributor scoped to the virtual network, which allows read, write and delete on its subnets and on every other network resource
Contributor scoped to the virtual network, which allows read, write and delete on its subnets and on every other resource type
Reader scoped to the virtual network, which allows read-only access to its subnets and to every other network resource

explanation.correct: A custom role scoped to the virtual network is the only arrangement that can carry exactly the subnet permissions the engineer needs — read, write and delete on subnets, join for moving virtual machines into or out of a subnet, and joinViaServiceEndpoint for switching on a service endpoint — while leaving out the permissions that would let the account delete `hub-vnet` itself or change its peerings. The built-in roles either carry the broader rights that the requirements forbid or the narrower rights that block the required work.

perChoice.slot0:b: Network Contributor carries read, write and delete rights over all network resources in scope, so this arrangement would also let the engineer remove `hub-vnet` and work with its peerings, which the requirements rule out.
perChoice.slot0:c: Contributor grants read, write and delete on every resource type in scope, including `hub-vnet` itself, so it is far broader than the duties the engineer actually performs.
perChoice.slot0:d: Reader is read-only, so the engineer could not create, change or remove subnets, move virtual machines into or out of them, or switch on a service endpoint.

body.stem: You administer the virtual network `corp-vnet` in East US 2 (subscription Contoso-Prod). The IPAM team has asked for the `data` subnet to use the address range 10.10.2.0/24, and the two Linux virtual machines and the private endpoint in `data` must keep serving traffic with their data intact and must still be hosted in `data` once the work is done. Azure rejects the request and the range of `data` stays 10.10.1.0/24. Which sequence of actions should you carry out to apply the new range, and which check should you make if Azure still refuses the change afterwards?

exhibit.text:
Setting                                Current value
---------------------------------------  ------------------------------------------------------------------
Region and subscription of corp-vnet     East US 2, Contoso-Prod
Address space of corp-vnet               10.10.0.0/16
Address range of subnet data             10.10.1.0/24
Contents of subnet data                  2 Linux virtual machines (web-01, web-02) and 1 private
                                        endpoint for Azure Storage
Address range of subnet web              10.10.10.0/24
Contents of subnet web                   1 Linux virtual machine (api-01)

body.statement: You should {{slot1}}, and if Azure still refuses the change afterwards you should {{slot2}}.

options.text: Move the workloads in `data` to a temporary subnet of `corp-vnet`, change the address range of `data` to 10.10.2.0/24, and then move the workloads back into `data`.
Delete the workloads in `data`, change the address range of `data` to 10.10.2.0/24, and then recreate the workloads as new virtual machines in `data`.
Add a range of 10.10.2.0/24 to the address space of `corp-vnet` and change the address range of `data` to 10.10.2.0/24 while the workloads stay in place.
Move the workloads in `data` to the `web` subnet of `corp-vnet`, change the address range of `data` to 10.10.2.0/24, and then leave the workloads in `web`, which becomes a permanent home for them.
Check whether gateway connections, gateways, IP resources, virtual network peerings, or an App Service Environment are blocking the subnet operation.
Check whether the resource group that holds `corp-vnet` carries a deny assignment on subnet write operations.
Check whether the virtual network quota for the subscription has been reached and request an increase if a limit has been exhausted.
Check whether the delegation list of the `data` subnet names a service that must be removed before the range can be edited.

explanation.correct: An existing subnet only accepts a new address range while nothing is deployed in it, so the workloads have to leave `data` first. The keyed sequence moves them to a temporary subnet of `corp-vnet` (a free, non-overlapping range inside the network's address space, such as 10.10.3.0/24), changes the range of `data` to 10.10.2.0/24, and moves them back so that `data` keeps hosting the two virtual machines and the private endpoint; the exact steps for relocating a given resource type differ, for example a private endpoint is recreated with a network interface in the target subnet. If the change is still refused, the documentation lists the connections that can block adding, changing or deleting a subnet: gateway connections, gateways, IPs, virtual network peerings, and an App Service Environment (ASE), which is exactly what the keyed check looks for.

perChoice.slot1:b: Deleting the workloads does free the subnet, and Azure does allow the range to be edited once nothing is deployed in it, but this breaks the stated requirement that the two virtual machines and the private endpoint keep running with their current data: the instances would have to be torn down and rebuilt and the private endpoint recreated from scratch.
perChoice.slot1:c: 10.10.2.0/24 already sits inside the address space of `corp-vnet`, so adding it to the network changes nothing, and a network-level range does not unlock a subnet-level edit: Azure only accepts a new subnet address range while the subnet holds no resources, so the workloads would have to leave first.
perChoice.slot1:d: This does apply the new range to `data`, but the workloads end up hosted in `web` instead of `data`, which does not meet the requirement that they remain hosted in `data` once the work is done.
perChoice.slot2:b: A deny assignment at resource group scope can block writes in practice, but it is not the list of connections named for a failed subnet add, change or delete: gateway connections, gateways, IPs, virtual network peerings, and an App Service Environment.
perChoice.slot2:c: Networking quotas are raised through a quota request, but a subnet address range edit is not refused because a quota limit was reached; the documented blockers for a failed subnet operation are gateway connections, gateways, IPs, virtual network peerings, and an App Service Environment.
perChoice.slot2:d: Delegations only have to be cleared before you change the delegations of a subnet, not before you change its address range, and a delegation is not listed as a blocker for this operation; the documented blockers are gateway connections, gateways, IPs, virtual network peerings, and an App Service Environment.
